title: Jeep Comanche MJ
verdict: A Cherokee XJ from the B-pillar forward and a fully boxed truck frame behind it. Give it the 4.0 six and a Dana 44 and it will carry a ton. About 190,000 were built, Chrysler had little reason to keep it once Dodge had the Dakota, and now the bed, tailgate and taillights are harder to find than the truck. Pull up the carpet before you pull out your wallet.

paragraphs: AMC unveiled the Comanche in August 1985 to more than 1,500 dealers in the ballroom of the MGM Grand in Las Vegas. It was a compact pickup built from the [[jeep/cherokee-xj|Cherokee XJ]]: the same unibody, Quadra-Link coil front end and engines from the cab forward, and behind the cab a fully boxed frame and a removable bed. At $7,049 for a two-wheel-drive model it was the cheapest Jeep of 1986. It lasted seven model years and 190,446 trucks, and it was Jeep's last pickup until the [[jeep/gladiator-jt|Gladiator]] 27 years later.

story.heading: A CHEROKEE WITH A TRUCK BOLTED ON
paragraphs: AMC needed money and needed a truck. Its finances were weak, a new Canadian plant was being built for the Eagle Premier, and compact pickups were selling. The answer was cheap to engineer: keep the XJ's front half and its 'Uniframe' unibody, and graft on a frame for the bed. Wikipedia describes that rear structure as fully boxed rather than the usual open C-channel, with rails more than eight inches deep and a large X-member over the rear axle. AMC had first tried the idea on its 1971 'Cowboy' pickup prototype.

The long-bed, seven-foot truck came first, for 1986. A six-foot short bed followed for 1987, on a 113-inch wheelbase against 119.9 inches for the long bed. Up front was the XJ's coil-sprung Dana 30 (or a beam axle on 2WD trucks). At the back were rear leaf springs much longer than the Cherokee's and, as standard, a Dana 35. The Metric Ton package for long beds added heavier springs, wheels and tires and a Dana 44, raising payload from 1,400 to 2,205 lb. Wikipedia notes that this was more than many full-size pickups could carry.

story.heading: FROM A WEAK V6 TO THE 4.0
paragraphs: 1986 Comanches had AMC's 2.5-liter four, a carbureted GM 2.8 V6 that made slightly less power than the four, or a Renault 2.1 turbodiesel. For 1987 the 4.0-liter straight-six arrived with 173 hp and 220 lb-ft, about 50% more power than the V6, together with the Aisin AW4 automatic and the NP231 Command-Trac and NP242 Selec-Trac transfer cases. Chrysler bought AMC in March 1987 and mostly left the truck alone. It gained an eight-slot grille for 1988, the sporty Eliminator trim, and the Aisin AX-15 five-speed in place of the Peugeot BA-10/5 during 1989.

For 1991 Chrysler replaced the Renix engine management with its own, and the 4.0 became the 190 hp 'High Output'. Quadratec's fitment listings also show Chrysler 8.25-inch rear axles in 1991–92 trucks. By then, though, the truck had stopped selling. Calendar-year output fell from 43,718 in 1988 to 5,188 in 1991. Jeep-Eagle dealers asked Chrysler to drop it and give them a Dakota-based pickup instead, and Chrysler wanted Jeep to sell SUVs and Dodge to sell trucks. The last Comanche left Toledo on June 12, 1992.

story.heading: WHY THEY'RE WORTH SAVING
paragraphs: Today the Comanche is the [[jeep/cherokee-xj|XJ]]'s rarer, more useful sibling. Comanche Club members got vehicle-in-operation figures from Key Parts showing about 18,600 MJs registered in the US and Canada in late 2021, roughly a tenth of production. Mechanically it is the XJ: the same 4.0, AX-15 and AW4, Dana 30 and NP231, so the drivetrain parts aren't hard to find. The cab interior and everything behind the doors are a different story. Bed sides, tailgates, taillights and bench-seat sliders are MJ-only and getting scarce.

On the trail it behaves like a long Cherokee with a bigger rear overhang. The XJ front suspension, the 4.0 and the easy 4WD conversions owners talk about make it a natural budget builder, and a Metric Ton or 8.25-axle truck has the rear end to carry a camper shell full of gear. Like the [[jeep/cj-8|CJ-8 Scrambler]], it suits owners who want a Jeep with a bed. The modern equivalent is the [[jeep/jl-unlimited|JL Unlimited]]-based Gladiator.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · THE NAME THAT DIDN'T COME BACK
callout.title: Comanche, Scrambler or Gladiator?
paragraphs: When Jeep returned to pickups for 2020, Wikipedia says it considered reviving the Comanche name alongside Scrambler before choosing Gladiator. It suggests the Comanche name's weaker recognition, and sensitivity to the Comanche Nation, likely counted against it.

AMC had other plans for the MJ. When it was setting up Beijing Jeep, it brought Chinese officials into the negotiations with the aim of building and selling Comanches there too. Wikipedia says the aim was to build and sell Comanches in China through the venture. In the end, Beijing Jeep became known for the Cherokee, which it built for decades.

engineering_intro: The MJ is an XJ Cherokee from the B-pillar forward: welded unibody, Quadra-Link coil front suspension with four control arms and a track bar, and the same engines and transfer cases. Behind the cab, a fully boxed rear frame with a large X-member over the axle carries a removable bed on long leaf springs. Two wheelbases, 113 in (six-foot bed, from 1987) and 119.9 in (seven-foot bed), share the cab.

engineering.v: XJ unibody front, boxed rear frame with X-member
engineering.note: Rails over 8 in deep. NAXJA members say the rear rails are part of the unibody, not bolted on.

engineering.v: Quadra-Link: coils, 4 control arms, track bar
engineering.note: Same as the XJ. 4WD trucks have a Dana 30; 2WD trucks a beam axle.
Longer than the Cherokee's. XJ axles aren't drop-in: the spring widths differ.
The Metric Ton package brings the Dana 44. Offroaders lists an AMC 20 as a 1986 heavy-duty option.
2.61:1 low range in 1986, 2.72:1 after. NP231 is part-time; NP242 adds full-time 4WD.

buying_checks.head: Pull up the carpet
buying_checks.body: NAXJA and Comanche Club members agree: rust is the number-one issue, and unless the truck lived in the Southwest or Southern California, expect it in the floors. Rusty seat brackets or bolts usually mean rusty floor pans below.

buying_checks.head: Check where the cab meets the bed, and the rails
buying_checks.body: Look hard where the bed meets the cab and where the unibody joins the rear frame. NAXJA members warn that bulging rail bottoms mean rust inside. Water also enters through the rear cab bulkhead and window; one member says more than one MJ has gone to the crusher because of it.

buying_checks.head: Look for cracks and old welds on the frame
buying_checks.body: Comanche Club members say to inspect the frame closely for cracks or signs of weld repair, especially on trucks that hauled or towed.

buying_checks.head: Bed, tailgate and taillights
buying_checks.body: These are MJ-only parts and hard to replace. A crushed bed side or a missing tailgate costs more and takes longer to fix than a tired engine.

buying_checks.head: Identify the rear axle
buying_checks.body: An oval cover usually means a Dana 35, and an angular, roughly hexagonal cover means a Dana 44, per NAXJA. A 1991–92 truck may have the Chrysler 8.25. Ask whether it's a Metric Ton truck; sellers often don't know.

buying_checks.head: Renix or HO?
buying_checks.body: 1987–90 4.0s run Renix management, which stores no codes and is diagnosed with a multimeter. 1991–92 HO trucks have Chrysler's system and 190 hp. Both are good engines, but Renix trucks reward owners who like electrical troubleshooting.

buying_checks.head: Hydraulic clutch and fuse box
buying_checks.body: On manual trucks, check the clutch master cylinder. Comanche Club members warn a leak can drip brake fluid into the fuse box, which damages it.

buying_checks.head: 2.5 or 4.0?
buying_checks.body: The 4.0 is the one to have. If you buy a 2.5, Comanche Club members suggest looking for a 4.10 or 4.56 axle ratio. The AX-4 and AX-5 gearboxes behind the 2.5 won't bolt up to a 4.0.

repairs.title: Replace rusted floor pans and rockers
repairs.symptoms: Wet carpet, rusty seat-bracket bolts, holes under the mats, crumbling rockers, and rust at the rear cab bulkhead where the bed meets the cab.
repairs.fix: Strip the cab, cut out the rot to clean metal, and treat what you can't cut. Trial-fit the panels, then plug- or stitch-weld them in. On a unibody, the floor and rockers are structural, so don't rely on screwed-in tin. Seam-seal, paint and wax the cavities. Fix the leak that caused it, usually the rear window and bulkhead seals. If the rails under the cab are swollen with rust, the job is much bigger.
repairs.tools: MIG welder · cut-off wheel · spot-weld drill · clamps · weld-through primer · seam sealer · cavity wax

repairs.title: Replace a leaking clutch master cylinder
repairs.cost: A master cylinder or master kit
repairs.symptoms: A soft or sinking clutch pedal, fluid on the firewall, or electrical faults from fluid dripping into the fuse box below. Comanche Club members also recommend checking the clutch-pedal welds, which some owners found incomplete and cracked.
repairs.fix: Clean any brake fluid off the fuse box and connectors right away. Disconnect the pushrod at the pedal, unbolt the master cylinder from the firewall and remove it with the line. Bleed the hydraulics after fitting, following the part's instructions. Check the pedal pivot and welds while you're under the dash.
repairs.tools: Sockets and extensions · flare-nut wrench · flashlight · brake cleaner · DOT 3 fluid

repairs.title: Hot stalls and no-starts: CPS, ballast resistor, grounds
repairs.cost: A sensor or resistor plus your time
repairs.symptoms: The engine dies when hot and won't restart until it cools, cranks without spark, or the fuel pump won't run. Comanche Club owners name the crankshaft position sensor (CPS) and the Renix fuel-pump ballast resistor as the usual culprits, and say to check the body grounds first for strange electrical faults.
repairs.fix: Test before you buy. Clean and tighten the engine, body and taillight grounds, and the ground at the fuel tank. Then test the CPS hot, right after a failure, with a multimeter against the resistance values for your year. On Renix trucks, check the ballast resistor; a jumper wire from the battery to the pump circuit will prove it at the roadside. Replace the failed part with one for your exact year, because the parts changed for the 1991 HO system.
repairs.tools: Self-ranging multimeter · wire brush · dielectric grease · long extensions

repairs.title: Reseal the oil filter adapter
repairs.symptoms: Oil on the driver's side of the block and dripping off the crossmember. Comanche Club members warn that a bad adapter O-ring is often misdiagnosed as a rear main seal.
repairs.fix: Clean the engine so you can see where the leak starts. Drain the oil, remove the filter, unbolt the adapter, clean both faces, fit new O-rings and refit. Use the 1987–92 O-rings for the MJ's 4.0. Note that Renix-era engines use a metric filter thread; a Comanche Club write-up covers converting to an SAE filter.
repairs.tools: Sockets · filter wrench · drain pan · degreaser · rags

repairs.title: Sort out the cooling system (and the Renix closed system)
repairs.symptoms: Overheating on hills or in traffic, coolant loss, or a cracked pressurized plastic coolant bottle. Comanche Club members suggest replacing the plastic bottle with an aluminum one, or converting the 1987–90 Renix closed system to the later open layout.
repairs.fix: Start cheap: test the cap, thermostat, fan clutch and electric fan, and clean the temperature-sender contacts. Pressure-test for leaks. Replace a cracked bottle and tired hoses, and the water pump if it weeps. If you convert a Renix truck to the open system, follow a documented write-up, such as Cruiser54's on Comanche Club, and bleed the system fully afterward.
repairs.tools: Cooling-system pressure tester · fan-clutch wrench · drain pan · funnel kit

repairs.title: Rebush the rear leaf springs and shackles
repairs.symptoms: Clunks over bumps, a rear end that steers itself, rusted or seized shackles, or bent lower shock-mount bolts. Comanche Club owners recommend upgrading the rear lower shock mounts.
repairs.fix: Support the frame and take the weight off the springs. Soak every bolt in penetrant for a few days first. Unbolt the shackles and front hangers, drop each spring, press out the old bushings and fit new ones (polyurethane needs grease). Fit new shackles, torque everything at ride height, and replace the shocks while you're there.
repairs.tools: Jack stands · penetrating oil · bushing press or vise · torque wrench

repairs.title: Fix or bypass the front axle disconnect (CAD)
repairs.symptoms: 4WD that engages at the transfer case but doesn't drive the front wheels, or grinding from the front axle. Comanche Club members say to check the vacuum-operated central axle disconnect before your first trail, and to lock it in or bypass it if necessary.
repairs.fix: Check the vacuum lines and the switch on the transfer case first. If the shift motor or fork is the problem, a manual disconnect kit replaces the vacuum actuator with a cable or lever, or the axle can be made permanently engaged with the right parts. Drain the gear oil, unbolt the shift-motor housing, fit the kit and refill with 75W-90.
repairs.tools: Vacuum gauge or hand pump · sockets · gasket scraper · RTV · gear oil

repairs.title: Cure death wobble: track bar and steering
repairs.symptoms: Violent front shake after a bump at speed, wandering and clunks. The MJ front end is the XJ's, with the same weak points: the track bar, tie-rod ends, drag link and steering box.
repairs.fix: With the engine running, have a helper turn the wheel back and forth while you watch the track-bar ends and bracket, the tie-rod and drag-link ends and the steering box for movement. Replace worn parts (an adjustable track bar re-centers a lifted axle), tighten everything at ride height, and check the unibody around the steering box for cracks. A steering stabilizer hides wobble; it doesn't cure it.
repairs.tools: Helper · pry bar · tie-rod puller · torque wrench · alignment afterward

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: The MJ's front end and fenders are the XJ's, so XJ consensus is a fair guide: a 235/75R15 (about 29 in) on the stock 15 in wheels fits, and a 30x9.50R15 is the practical limit, possibly rubbing the front lower control arms at full lock. NAXJA posters say a 31x10.50 needs bump stops or trimming. We found no separate MJ-only consensus. Load the bed before judging rear clearance.

faq.q: Which years and engines should I buy?
faq.a: Buy a 4.0. 1991–92 HO trucks have 190 hp and Chrysler's easier-to-diagnose engine management. 1987–90 Renix trucks are good too, but they're diagnosed with a multimeter. 1986 trucks have no 4.0. If you do buy a 2.5, look for 4.10 or 4.56 gears.

faq.q: What is a Metric Ton Comanche?
faq.a: A long-bed heavy-duty package with heavier leaf springs, wheels and tires and a Dana 44 rear axle. It raised payload from 1,400 to 2,205 lb. Sellers often don't know they have one, so check the axle and springs.

faq.q: Which rear axle do I have?
faq.a: The Dana 35 was standard. The Dana 44 came with the Metric Ton package (and on some other trucks; Comanche Club members' trucks include a 1992 short bed with a limited-slip Dana 44). Offroaders lists an AMC 20 as a 1986 heavy-duty option, and Quadratec's locker fitment shows the 27-spline Chrysler 8.25 on 1991–92 trucks. NAXJA: oval cover means Dana 35; angular, roughly hexagonal cover means Dana 44.

The six-foot short bed rides on a 113 in wheelbase and arrived for 1987. The seven-foot long bed is on 119.9 in and was the only length in 1986. The short bed is better on tight trails; Metric Ton trucks are long beds. The Eliminator was short-bed only, per Comanche Club.
Under the carpet, at the rear cab bulkhead and window seals, where the bed meets the cab, and where the unibody meets the rear frame. NAXJA members say bulging rail bottoms mean rust inside.

Drivetrain and front-end parts are shared with the XJ and easy to find. Comanche Club members say everything behind the doors is different, and the bed, tailgate, taillights and bench-seat sliders are MJ-specific and scarce. An XJ fuel pump and sender don't fit without fabrication.

faq.q: How much can it tow and carry?
faq.a: Kelley Blue Book lists a 1992 Comanche at 5,000 lb maximum towing and 1,475 lb payload. Wikipedia gives 1,400 lb for a standard truck and 2,205 lb for the Metric Ton package.
From 1987 the NP231 Command-Trac is part-time and the NP242 Selec-Trac adds a full-time 4WD mode. Both have 2.72:1 low range. 1986 trucks used the NP207 and NP228, both with 2.61:1 low range.

faq.q: Why does my MJ stall when hot?
faq.a: Usually the crankshaft position sensor, which can fail when hot and test fine cold, or, on Renix trucks, the fuel-pump ballast resistor. Comanche Club members say to check the body grounds first for any strange electrical fault.
AMC and Chrysler built 190,446. Comanche Club members got 2021 vehicle-in-operation figures from Key Parts showing about 18,600 registered in the US and Canada.
